targetQuery: virtual memory paging page tables TLB page faults working set vs committed vs virtual memory C#
comparedAgainst: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/memory/about-memory-management, /virtual-address-space, /working-set, /reserving-and-committing-memory — Microsoft's own conceptual pages on this exact topic. Fetched live: they explain the mechanism (page tables, working set, commit) but never measure it on a running process; a reader is left with diagrams and prose only, no way to see the three numbers actually diverge.

Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, ch. 18 'Paging: Introduction' and ch. 19 'Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs)' (pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP) — fetched and converted to text with pdftotext (WebFetch's own PDF rendering silently returned nothing useful; pdftotext in Git Bash worked). This is the standard textbook treatment: PTE fields, the TLB hit/miss path, and the ch. 19 homework's own hardware microbenchmark.

General category comparison: typical 'what is virtual memory' explainers (GeeksforGeeks-tier, and even much of Microsoft Learn's own conceptual set) stop at labelled diagrams. This article's differentiator — driving Process.WorkingSet64/PrivateMemorySize64/VirtualMemorySize64 apart with a live VirtualAlloc/VirtualFree demo and showing MemoryMappedFile page-sharing with real IOException output — is genuinely not something I found duplicated at this depth in the compared sources. That differentiation is real and is the article's main strength.
justification: node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/operating-systems/virtual-memory.md was run three times from PowerShell; all three passed identically (PASS, blocks=10, executed=5), no flakiness. I did not stop at trusting the harness: I extracted all five run blocks (commit-vs-workingset, decommit-half, mmf-two-views, mmf-collision, mmf-fix) into standalone .cs files and ran each with `dotnet run` myself outside the harness, on this same machine (.NET SDK here reports 10.0.401, matching the article's stated toolchain exactly). Results: (1) the VirtualAlloc/VirtualFree demo's causal claims hold up exactly as described — reserving 200 MB moved only the virtual figure (+199 MB), left private and working-set essentially flat; committing moved only private (+201 MB), leaving virtual and working-set flat; touching every page moved only working-set (+200 MB), leaving virtual and private flat; freeing brought all three back down together. My own run's numbers (RAM 63.9 GB, page size 4,096 bytes, baseline 2,233,455 MB virtual / 6 MB private / 19 MB working set) landed within 1 MB of the article's own quoted baseline (2,233,454/6/19), which is strong evidence the article's numbers are genuinely measured on this machine, not invented. (2) The decommit-half exercise solution reproduced the article's exact claimed deltas: private 206->106 MB, working set 217->119 MB, virtual moving only a few tens of MB (29 MB in my run) because the reservation itself was never released. (3) The memory-mapped-file demo: `readerView` really does see `writerView`'s writes with zero explicit copy (int 42, the UTF-8 string, and the same bytes on disk after dispose), confirming the two-views-share-physical-pages claim. (4) The CreateNew collision demo reproduces the exact real .NET exception message ('IOException: Cannot create a file when that file already exists.'), and CreateOrOpen genuinely fixes it. All demos are robust across repeated runs; nothing here is fragile. Sourcing is unusually rigorous: I independently re-fetched every Microsoft Learn API page cited (WorkingSet64, PrivateMemorySize64, VirtualMemorySize64, the Working Set and Reserving-and-Committing conceptual pages, About Memory Management, Virtual Address Space, Memory-Mapped Files) and every quoted sentence matches the live page verbatim, including the 8 TB address-space figure, the working-set/private/virtual-bytes performance-counter equivalences, the hard-vs-soft/demand-zero fault taxonomy, and the 'committed pages do not consume any physical storage until they are first accessed' line. None of the three Process properties are conflated or mislabeled: WorkingSet64 = resident physical pages (Working Set counter), PrivateMemorySize64 = non-shareable committed memory (Private Bytes counter), VirtualMemorySize64 = full reserved+committed address space (Virtual Bytes counter) — this is exactly what the docs say. I also converted the two cited OSTEP PDFs to text with pdftotext and checked the specific claims directly: ch. 18's PTE description (valid bit, protection bits, present bit, dirty and accessed/reference bits, PFN) matches the chapter's own Figure 18.5 description of the x86 PTE word for word in substance; ch. 19's homework section states, verbatim, 'The overall difference between hits in the first-level TLB and misses is quite large, roughly a factor of fourteen' — the article's 'roughly fourteen times' claim, hedged as specific to that measurement and hardware, is an exact and honestly-scoped match, not an invented number. The writer's decision to hedge away from asserting Task Manager's exact column label (item 7 of this brief) is the right call: Task Manager's Details-tab memory columns (Working Set (Memory), Private Working Set, Commit Size, etc.) don't all map one-to-one onto the three Process properties, and grounding the precise equivalences in the PerfMon counter names instead (which the docs do state exactly: Working Set, Private Bytes, Virtual Bytes) is both defensible and avoids an unverifiable UI-string claim; it leaves no real gap since the load-bearing claims are the ones actually verified. However, I did find one demonstrable numerical error, which under this project's rubric caps the score: in the closing section ('Does a multi-terabyte virtual figure mean...') the article states the baseline VirtualMemorySize64 (2,233,454 MB, per the article's own earlier measurement) was 'already tens of thousands of times the installed RAM' given a machine with 63.9 GB of RAM (also the article's own number, stated in the same sentence). 63.9 GB = 65,433.6 MB, and 2,233,454 / 65,433.6 is approximately 34 - the virtual figure is about 34 times the available RAM, not tens of thousands of times (off by roughly three orders of magnitude; 34,953 is what you get if you divide the MB figure by the bare number 63.9 without converting GB to MB first, which is almost certainly the arithmetic error that produced this line). A related, softer version of the same confusion appears a few paragraphs earlier: 'the huge virtual figure is most of the 8 TB address space the process could in principle reserve' - 2,233,454 MB is about 2.13 TB, roughly 27% of an 8 TB space, not 'most' of it (which implies a majority). Both sentences are about the article's own two headline demonstration numbers (the baseline virtual figure vs. installed RAM, and the baseline virtual figure vs. the 8 TB ceiling), so a careful reader who does the arithmetic the article invites them to do will catch the same inconsistency I did. Everything else checked out; this is otherwise the strongest-sourced, most rigorously self-verified article of this kind I compared against, and the fix is a two-sentence numeric correction, not a rewrite.

issues.location: Final section, 'Does a multi-terabyte "virtual" figure mean the machine is almost out of memory?', the sentence "the virtual number was already tens of thousands of times the installed RAM."
issues.problem: Using the article's own numbers from the same sentence (2,233,454 MB baseline virtual, 63.9 GB RAM available to the GC), the ratio is roughly 34x (2,233,454 MB / 65,433.6 MB), not 'tens of thousands' of times. The stated figure is off by roughly three orders of magnitude, which is exactly what you'd get by dividing the MB figure by the bare GB number (63.9) instead of converting GB to MB first. This is a factual/arithmetic error in the article's own headline conclusion, not a nitpick about wording.
issues.fixLooksLike: Recompute: 2,233,454 MB / (63.9 * 1024) MB = ~34.9x. Change the sentence to something like 'the virtual number was already around 35 times the installed RAM' (or restate qualitatively as 'tens of times', which is accurate, rather than 'tens of thousands of times', which is not). Double-check the companion sentence a few paragraphs earlier ('the huge virtual figure is most of the 8 TB address space') at the same time: 2,233,454 MB is about 2.13 TB, roughly a quarter of 8 TB, not 'most' of it — reword to 'a meaningful slice of' or similar and drop 'most'.
